thesis: The index add restored the price without fixing the business problem. RDDT fell 11% on 2026-07-30 when Q2 revenue rose 61% to $805M but US daily actives went backwards sequentially (53.5M in Q1 to 53.2M in Q2, +6% YoY) and management called Google search referrals choppy, with AI Overviews cutting referral clicks and data-licensing renewals with Google and OpenAI on no clear timeline. The stock traded 153-158 for the first two weeks of August, then jumped 12.6% on Aug 14 purely on the S&P announcement, landing at 178.09 — right back on its 200-day SMA of 177.86 with nothing about the DAU trend changed. Forced index demand is a one-day liquidity event; from Tuesday the marginal buyer is gone and the July de-rating range is unguarded.
key_risk: Shorting a 6.88% daily ATR name into an index event. A data-licensing renewal with Google or OpenAI announced at any time would squeeze this violently, and the stop at 197 is only 1.5 ATR above the entry — well inside the noise band for this ticker. Size small and treat the stop as absolute.
counter_argument: The classic index-effect fade has decayed badly over the last decade because it is the most front-run trade in the market, and the Aug 14 move may already BE the front-running rather than the thing to fade. The business is also genuinely good — 61% revenue growth, 43% adjusted EBITDA margin, EPS $1.25 against a $0.96 estimate — so this is a valuation-and-flow short, not a broken-company short. If the tape stays at all-time highs and the bull market keeps broadening, a 32%-off-high growth name is the wrong thing to be short.

catalyst.action: STAND DOWN. This is an UPDATE to the two open XLE entries (60.80 from 08-15 and 60.50 from 08-16) — neither filled; Friday low was 61.25. CANCEL both working orders. thesis: The thesis is intact but the price ran away from the order and the entry no longer exists. XLE gapped from 57.50 to 60.18 on Aug 10 when Hormuz reopening talks collapsed and has closed higher every session since to 61.91 — the two open entries at 60.50/60.80 sat below that and never filled. What is left is a headline-driven risk premium, +21.6% YTD, sitting 2.4% under its 200-day range high of 63.46, hostage to a binary that resolves today. The underlying physical tightness is real (IEA Q3 deficit 1.8 mb/d, US commercial crude below the 5-year low through end-2026), which is why this is a wait rather than a cancel-and-forget.
key_risk: Chasing here is the risk. A credible ceasefire extension or reopening framework out of today deadline gaps XLE back toward 57.50-58.50 as fast as it gapped up, and every major sell-side house already forecasts Brent BELOW spot by Q4 — Goldman ~80, JPMorgan ~80, EIA STEO 69 for 2027.
counter_argument: Waiting for the gap fill may mean never getting filled. Capital Economics argues a strait closed through Q4 takes crude to 120-140 as OECD inventory buffers exhaust, and the IEA revision is genuine physical tightening rather than pure premium — in that path XLE goes to 68 without ever revisiting 59, and this update costs the whole move. The counter to the counter: a fresh entry at 61.91 against a 58.60 stop and a 64.50 target is 0.78 reward-to-risk, and even the 67.00 target is only 1.54. There is no version of buying here that clears the 2.0 swing floor.

thesis: Position update, not a new idea. The bear case has strengthened since Sunday: spot ETFs have now bled four straight sessions for ~$385M, and BTC has spent the last week failing to reclaim 64,500 while the whole crypto complex barely moves (ETH +1.1%, SOL +0.4%, DOGE +0.7% over 24h — no leadership anywhere). The macro leg is the real driver: with three July FOMC dissents for a hike and an oil-driven inflation impulse, the marginal dollar is not going into a zero-yield asset. Late-June already printed a 21-month low near 58,000 on the same combination of a cautious Fed and roughly $4B of June ETF outflows, so the path to the target is one the tape has walked recently.
key_risk: Coiled ranges resolve violently in whichever direction they resolve. Sellers have not managed sub-60,000 and buyers will not lift 64,500, and that equilibrium usually breaks with a volatility spike — the 65,200 stop is only 2.8% above spot, so a single risk-on headline out of the Iran deadline takes it out before the thesis gets a chance.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is simply the tape everywhere else: SPX and the Russell 2000 are at all-time highs and the bull market is broadening. Being short the highest-beta risk asset in a broadening bull market is fighting the dominant trend, and $385M of outflows is small against a multi-hundred-billion asset — it is a sentiment reading, not a supply shock. If Jackson Hole lands dovish, 58,000 will not print.

thesis: Uranium is the only energy-security asset that de-rated during an actual energy-security crisis, and it de-rated on the wrong price. CCJ is 27.7% off its 200-day high of 135.24 and below its 200-day SMA, while the long-term contract price that actually sets Cameco realised revenue sits at $95.50/lb, the top of its 12-month range. The selloff traces to spot cooling from January, sector risk-off in high-beta uranium names, and a company-specific growth pause — 2026 deliveries guided to 29-32 Mlbs against 33 Mlbs in 2025 — plus a Q2 optically weak only because 2025 contained a one-time Westinghouse contribution. Underneath, adjusted EBITDA was $391M, five-year contract coverage averages over 28 Mlbs a year, and new contracts are being written with escalated floors in the high $70s, which puts a contractual floor under the realised price that did not exist in the last cycle.
key_risk: Cameco is a mining company and the near-term repricing is about mining risk, not uranium risk: the northern Saskatchewan operations (McArthur River, Cigar Lake) carry real operating and logistics uncertainty, and a genuine production problem there would cut deliveries below the contracted book and force Cameco to buy in the spot market to fill contracts — the one scenario where a high uranium price actively hurts the company.
counter_argument: INVALIDATION (this is the required condition, not a price move): the thesis is wrong if the long-term contract price prints below $80/lb for two consecutive quarterly readings, or if Cameco guides 2027 deliveries below 28 Mlbs and breaks its own five-year coverage average. Either would mean utilities have stopped locking in supply and the tight-balance story is over. Beyond that: the honest bear case is that the DOE $17.5B commitment is conditional and AP1000 pipelines have slipped for two decades, so paying up for 91 reactors of optionality is paying for a schedule that has never once been met. At $80 the stock is back to its 200-day low with only the contracted uranium business in the price — that is the bear-case anchor.

thesis: The market sold off-price apparel as an oil-shock consumer casualty when it is the structural beneficiary of exactly that shock. TJX fell 6.1% in six sessions from 162.06 on Aug 6 to 152.11 on Aug 14, tracking the Aug 10 crude spike tick for tick, and broke its 20-, 50- and 200-day SMAs in the process. But the selling came on lower volume than the advance that preceded it (3.9-5.4M a day versus 6.9-7.4M on the up days), which is sector beta rather than distribution, and the sell-side raised its EPS estimate into the print. The mechanism runs the other way from the price: a squeezed consumer trades down into off-price, and full-price retailers who over-ordered dump inventory into the channel on better buying terms, so an energy shock widens TJX merchandise margin rather than compressing it. Unlike the dollar stores, TJX customer is not the sub-$35k household that gasoline actually crushes.
key_risk: The 146.50 stop is 1.5 ATR below entry and does NOT protect against an earnings gap — TJX can open 5% lower on a guidance cut and the stop fills wherever it fills. That is the entire reason for half size before the print. A cautious full-year comp guide, which is what Home Depot and Target are also at risk of on Aug 18-19, would validate the market read rather than mine.
counter_argument: Six down sessions through three moving averages is not usually noise, and the market has repeatedly been early rather than wrong on retail. Insiders offer no support: zero open-market purchases against nine sales worth $32.5M over six months. The trade-down mechanism is also a lagging one — it shows up over two to four quarters, not in a July quarter reported in August, so the Aug 19 catalyst may simply not contain the evidence the thesis needs. And the whole consumer cluster reports within 48 hours (HD Aug 18, LOW/TGT Aug 19, WMT Aug 20), so a single bad read-through drags TJX regardless of its own numbers.

thesis: Volatility is priced at its cheapest level in 200 days precisely as the calendar stacks four binaries into ten sessions. VIXY at 18.63 sits 0.7% above its 200-day low of 18.50 and 52.6% below its high of 39.33, with UVXY confirming at 20.10 against a 20.03 low — this is a floor, not a drift. Against that, the S&P and the Russell 2000 are at all-time highs while the July FOMC split 9-3 with three dissents to HIKE, an oil shock is running through an economy that just printed one of the weakest payroll reports of the decade, and a brand-new and historically hawkish Fed chair gives his first Jackson Hole keynote on Aug 27-29. This is a hedge bought at the cheapest price available in ten months, not a directional bearish call — it is the one position in today set that pays if every other one is wrong at the same time.
key_risk: VIXY holds first- and second-month VIX futures and bleeds continuously in contango. If the next three weeks pass quietly, this loses money by construction — the 16.80 stop is likely to be reached by decay alone even if volatility never falls, which is exactly why the size is 1% and the time stop is hard-dated at Sep 2. It is not leveraged (UVXY is the 1.5x version and is deliberately not the instrument here), but roll decay alone makes it unownable beyond its catalyst window.
counter_argument: Buying volatility because it is cheap is one of the most reliably losing trades in the market — vol is usually cheap for the good reason that nothing happens, and the 200-day low is a level VIXY can sit on for months while decay grinds the position to nothing. Every catalyst listed is scheduled and therefore already in the options surface. The strongest version of the bear case: if the Iran deadline produces a ceasefire extension today, oil and equity vol both collapse together and this position is down 10% before the Fed events even arrive.

thesis: Four insiders bought Nike stock on the open market in the last six months — including CEO Elliott Hill, twice on 2026-04-13 at about $42.27, and board member Tim Cook, 25,000 shares on 2026-04-10 at $42.43 — for $3.73M against $1.37M of sales. The stock now trades at 40.73, roughly 4% BELOW what they paid. That is the specific configuration worth weighting: a cluster of distinct open-market buyers in a name the market has de-rated 41% from its 200-day high. The fundamentals say the de-rating is regional rather than structural. Greater China is down 16% and is the entire drag, while North America grew 9%, wholesale 24%, and Running 20% for the second consecutive quarter, and fiscal Q4 earnings beat estimates on revenue down only 1.1%. The market is pricing a permanently impaired brand; the segment data describes a company with one broken region and a core that has already turned.
key_risk: The turnaround is behind its own schedule and management says so — Hill has publicly admitted the restructuring is not moving as fast as planned and that full impact waits until early 2027. Greater China is not an inventory problem that clears in a quarter; it is a promotional cycle plus local competition, and a second year of double-digit declines there would mean the brand issue is structural after all, not regional.
counter_argument: INVALIDATION (required condition, not a price move): the thesis is wrong if North America revenue growth turns negative for two consecutive quarters, or if Greater China is still declining double digits four quarters from now — either would mean the problem was never regional. Beyond that, the honest weaknesses: the stock is 1.8% off its 200-day low, so this is a knife-catch, and buying a falling name because insiders bought it 4% higher is a thesis that has destroyed a great deal of capital in genuinely declining businesses. The softest number in this idea is the $32 bear anchor — it is judgment about where a failed-turnaround Nike trades, not a fetched figure, and at a $30 anchor instead the reward-to-risk is 2.50, exactly at the long-term floor rather than comfortably above it. Treat the 2.5 clearance as marginal.
